metaDescription: Understand janitorial surety bond coverage ($10k-$100k dishonesty limits) and compare $0.07-$0.15/sq ft office cleaning bids in our Cost Calculator.
excerpt: When an after-hours cleaning crew holds master keyfobs to your executive offices, standard general liability insurance will not cover missing laptops, petty cash, or proprietary hardware. Learn what janitorial surety bond coverage means, what it costs contractors, and what bond limits to mandate in your RFP.
quickAnswer: Janitorial surety bond coverage—technically structured as a Business Services Bond or Third-Party Employee Dishonesty Crime Policy—protects commercial office tenants and landlords against theft of money, laptops, electronics, or property committed by a cleaning contractor's employees on the client's premises. Depending on facility square footage and asset density, US offices require $10,000 to $100,000+ in surety bond coverage; this costs the cleaning contractor only $120 to $650 per year (less than 0.3% of contract revenue) and is fully absorbed inside standard cleaning rates of $0.07 to $0.15 per sq ft or $35 to $65 per labor hour.

blocks.text: What Does Janitorial Surety Bond Coverage Actually Mean?

When a commercial janitorial company advertises that its crews are 'Licensed, Insured, and Bonded,' many office managers assume those three words describe a single pool of protection. In reality, insurance and bonding cover completely opposite risks. A commercial general liability policy only pays for accidental bodily injury or accidental property damage—such as a cleaner tipping over a mop bucket that shorts out a lobby floor outlet. General liability explicitly excludes intentional criminal acts, including employee theft, burglary, and embezzlement.

Because commercial office cleaning occurs overwhelmingly after hours—when a 2- to 6-person evening crew holds master keycards, alarm PINs, and physical brass keys to executive suites, IT closets, and supply rooms—the tenant faces a unique vulnerability: third-party employee dishonesty. Janitorial surety bond coverage (most commonly underwritten as a Business Services Bond or a Third-Party Client Property Crime Policy endorsement) bridges that exact gap. It guarantees financial reimbursement to the client (the Obligee) if an employee of the cleaning company (the Principal) steals cash, laptops, monitors, inventory, or physical assets while servicing your facility, backed by a licensed surety insurer (the Surety).

blocks.title: First-Party vs. Third-Party Employee Dishonesty
blocks.text: A standard Employee Dishonesty policy only protects the cleaning company if its own bookkeeper steals from the cleaning company's bank account (first-party loss). For your office to be protected against theft of your laptops or equipment, the vendor's bond or crime policy must include a 'Third-Party Client Property' or 'Business Services Bond' insuring agreement.
How a Three-Party Janitorial Surety Bond Works Compared to Insurance

Unlike a traditional two-party insurance policy that spreads risk across a pool of policyholders, a surety bond is a three-party financial guarantee involving the Principal (the janitorial contractor), the Obligee (your company or property management entity), and the Surety (the bond underwriter). If a janitorial technician steals three engineering workstations valued at $9,500 during a Wednesday night shift and the theft is verified, the Surety reimburses you up to the bond penalty limit—and then exercises its legal right of indemnity to collect that $9,500 back from the janitorial company's owners.

Because the cleaning contractor remains financially liable to indemnify the surety company for any paid theft claim, surety bond underwriters require janitorial businesses to enforce strict pre-employment criminal background screening, I-9/E-Verify verification, and physical key-control logs. Requiring verifiable surety bond coverage in your RFP therefore serves a dual purpose: it provides a financial backstop for missing office assets and acts as an independent underwriting screen that filters out fly-by-night crews who do not background-check their evening staff.
Janitorial Surety Bond Cost Benchmarks and Recommended Limits by Office Type

One of the biggest myths in commercial facility procurement is that requiring a $25,000 or $100,000 janitorial surety bond will drive up your monthly cleaning cost. For a cleaning contractor with clean credit and documented W-2 employee background screening, janitorial Business Services Bonds are among the most affordable risk instruments in commercial contracting. Underwriting rates typically range from 0.5% to 1.5% of the bond limit per year across a roster of 5 to 25 employees.

blocks.text: Distinguishing Dishonesty Bonds from Bid and Performance Bonds

Facility managers must use precise terminology in their RFP documents so bidders do not confuse a Janitorial Dishonesty / Business Services Bond with a Public Works Contract Performance Bond. In private-sector commercial real estate (offices from 2,500 to 50,000+ sq ft), 95% of requests for a 'janitorial surety bond' refer to a Third-Party Employee Dishonesty / Business Services Bond ($25,000 to $100,000 limit) protecting client property against theft.

By contrast, government buildings, municipal transit facilities, and large university campuses frequently mandate a Bid Bond (guaranteeing the low bidder will sign the contract at their quoted price) and a Performance & Payment Bond equal to 100% of the annual contract value (guaranteeing the surety will fund a replacement contractor if the cleaning vendor goes bankrupt mid-year). While a $50,000 Employee Dishonesty Bond costs a contractor around $300 per year across all their clients, a 100% Contract Performance Bond on a $120,000 annual daily cleaning agreement (5x/week = 21.65 visits/month at 4.33 weeks/month, using the 0.90x frequency multiplier) costs 1.5% to 3.0% of the contract value ($1,800 to $3,600 per year) and is passed directly through to the client.
Securing Physical Consumables and Restroom Assets Alongside Bond Coverage

While a $50,000 janitorial surety bond protects against high-value theft of laptops, mobile devices, and office equipment, commercial property managers also face low-level pilferage and waste of facility consumables when paper and soap supplies are included in the contract ($0.012 to $0.025 per sq ft per visit) or stocked in unlocked janitorial closets. Because most commercial crime bonds carry a $500 to $1,000 per-occurrence deductible, small losses of paper cases or sanitizer refills fall below the bond claim threshold and must be controlled through tamper-resistant dispensing hardware.

Pairing contractual surety bond protection with locked, high-capacity wall dispensers eliminates daily pilferage and unauthorized refill loss. Standardizing your restrooms and elevator lobbies with the Georgia-Pacific Compact Vertical Coreless Toilet Paper Dispenser (featuring a keyed lock, ADA slim footprint, and 3,000-sheet dual coreless capacity), the Georgia-Pacific enMotion Impulse 8-Inch Compact Towel Dispenser (touchless 8-inch roll capacity powered by 4 D-cell batteries for kitchenettes and washrooms), and the GOJO PURELL ES8 Touch-Free Hand Sanitizer Dispenser (1200 mL capacity with Energy-on-the-Refill technology and At-a-Glance level visibility for reception desks) locks down consumable inventory while your janitorial bond covers high-value tenant assets.

items.name: Step 1: Specify 'Third-Party Employee Dishonesty / Business Services Bond' in the RFP
items.text: State the exact minimum dollar limit required ($25,000 for suites under 10,000 sq ft; $50,000 to $100,000 for 10,000+ sq ft offices) and explicitly specify that coverage must extend to client property on client premises.

items.name: Step 2: Verify the Bond Number and Active Term on the Certificate
items.text: Request either a separate Surety Bond Certificate or a Crime Policy listing in the 'Other' row on the ACORD 25 COI showing the policy number, effective dates, and third-party client property limit.

items.name: Step 3: Audit Key Control & Badge Access Protocols
items.text: Require the vendor to assign individually numbered electronic keyfobs to specific W-2 background-checked technicians rather than sharing a single anonymous master keycard among rotating workers.

faqs.q: Does a janitorial surety bond cover damage if a cleaner accidentally breaks a glass conference room partition?
faqs.a: No. Accidental damage to interior glass and conference partitions (which typically cost $15 to $35 per visit to clean) or office furniture is covered under the contractor's Commercial General Liability policy (specifically including Care, Custody, or Control property extensions). A janitorial surety bond (Business Services Bond) only covers intentional theft or dishonest acts committed by the contractor's employees.

faqs.q: How much janitorial surety bond coverage should a 12,000 sq ft office require?
faqs.a: For a 12,000 sq ft commercial office cleaned 3x to 5x per week (13.0 to 21.65 visits per month based on 4.33 weeks/month, at standard rates of $0.07 to $0.12 per sq ft), require a minimum $50,000 Third-Party Employee Dishonesty / Business Services Bond. If your office houses unlocked high-value laptops, prototypes, or medical/financial hardware, increase the requirement to $100,000.

faqs.q: Are 1099 independent subcontractors covered under a janitorial company's surety bond?
faqs.a: Almost never. Standard Business Services Bonds and ISO Commercial Crime policies explicitly define 'Employee' as a W-2 worker compensated via direct payroll whose labor the contractor directs and controls. If your janitorial vendor subcontracts your building to 1099 operators, any theft committed by those subcontractors is typically excluded from the prime vendor's bond.

faqs.q: What is a 'Conviction Clause' in a janitorial dishonesty bond and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Many basic surety bonds contain a 'Conviction Clause' stating that the surety company will only pay a theft claim after the accused janitorial employee is formally arrested and convicted in a criminal court—a process that can take 9 to 18 months. High-performing facility contracts require a Commercial Crime Third-Party endorsement that pays upon police report and preponderance of evidence (such as badge logs and security camera footage) without waiting for a criminal trial verdict.

faqs.q: Should we pay extra on our monthly janitorial invoice for a $25,000 or $50,000 surety bond?
faqs.a: No. A $25,000 to $50,000 Business Services Bond costs a commercial janitorial company only $150 to $350 per year across their entire multi-client workforce. That equates to just a few dollars per month per client and is already baked into standard commercial hourly rates ($35 to $65/hr) and per-square-foot benchmarks.
